title: Tone, precise word choice, jargon and slang
blurb: Set the right tone, replace slang, clichés, jargon and inflated words with precise ones, and use respectful, person-first language.
question: A testing center canceled an applicant's exam because of a website error. His draft email begins, “Your incompetent website ruined my week, so thanks a lot.” What is wrong with the tone, and what would a firm but courteous version say?

teach.body: Formally, tone is the writer's attitude toward the subject and the reader, created mainly through word choice (diction). Precise word choice means picking the word with the exact meaning and the right connotation for the audience. Plain English: the same message can sound angry, timid or professional depending on the words. On the TEAS, the best option is respectful, clear and specific, and it fits the reader.

head: Problem
Example
Better
teach.caption: Jargon is fine among specialists; it becomes a problem only when the reader does not share it.

teach.body: Vague: “The nurse did some stuff to help the patient.” Precise: “The nurse adjusted the pillows to ease the patient's back pain.” Replace things, stuff and a lot with the actual noun or number. Replace weak verb phrases (did a check of, made a decision) with one strong verb (checked, decided). Precise writing is not longer for its own sake; every word carries meaning.

teach.caption: Denotation is the dictionary meaning; connotation is the feeling a word carries. Choose the connotation that fits the purpose.

teach.note: Praise (a recommendation letter) needs the positive word; a neutral report needs the neutral one.

teach.caption: Professional writing avoids sarcasm, condescension, threats and exaggeration.

teach.body: Put the person before the condition (person-first language): “a person with diabetes,” not “a diabetic.” Describe equipment as something a person uses, not as a prison: “a patient who uses a wheelchair,” not “wheelchair-bound” or “confined to a wheelchair.” Say “has asthma,” not “suffers from asthma.” Use gender-neutral job titles (firefighter, police officer, chairperson, flight attendant), and mention age, race, gender or disability only when it is relevant.

teach.h: Scenario: Andre fixes his complaint email
teach.body: Nursing applicant Andre Wallace drafted: “Your incompetent website ruined my week, so thanks a lot.” It insults the reader, uses sarcasm and never asks for anything. Revised: “A website error canceled my TEAS appointment on April 9. Please reschedule my exam for the next available date. I can provide my confirmation number if needed.” The tone is firm (facts and a clear request) and courteous (please, an offer to help).

teach.text: Watch for options that are polite but useless (“Sorry to bother you, but maybe...”), and options that sound sophisticated but are inflated (“utilize the facilitation of a dialogue”). The TEAS rewards the clear, specific, respectful choice, not the fanciest or the most apologetic one.

items: Tone is the writer's attitude, created through word choice.
Replace slang, clichés, inflated words and vague words with precise, standard ones.
Jargon suits specialists only; explain or replace it for general readers.
Choose the connotation that fits the purpose (assertive, not pushy, in praise).
Complaints should be firm and courteous: state the problem and the request, no insults.
Use person-first, gender-neutral language and mention traits only when relevant.

summary: You can now judge tone and choose precise words with the right connotation for the reader. You can also replace slang, clichés, jargon and inflated wording, and rewrite labels into respectful, person-first and gender-neutral language.

A.q: Which sentence is most appropriate for a scholarship essay?
options: Volunteering at the shelter was a total game changer for me.
Volunteering at the shelter was, like, really eye-opening stuff.
Volunteering at the shelter changed how I view patient care.
Volunteering at the shelter was awesome and super cool to do.
A.why: It uses standard, precise language and says specifically what changed.

whyNot.0: Total game changer is slang and a cliché.
whyNot.1: Like and stuff are casual filler and vague.
whyNot.3: Awesome and super cool are slang and say nothing specific.

A.q: Which sentence uses person-first, respectful language?
options: The clinic offers weekly classes for people with diabetes.
The clinic offers weekly classes for diabetics in the area.
The clinic offers weekly classes for diabetes sufferers.
The clinic offers weekly classes for the diabetic population.
A.why: “People with diabetes” names the person first and the condition second.

whyNot.1: Diabetics labels people by their condition.
whyNot.2: Sufferers frames the condition as suffering, which is not neutral.
whyNot.3: “The diabetic population” still labels people by the condition.

A.q: Which sentence uses the most precise wording?
options: The nurse did some stuff to help the patient feel better.
The nurse did a lot of things for the patient's comfort today.
The nurse helped the patient out with various things.
The nurse adjusted the pillows to ease the patient's pain.
A.why: A strong verb (adjusted) and specific nouns (pillows, pain) say exactly what happened.

whyNot.0: Some stuff is vague and informal.
whyNot.1: A lot of things is vague; the reader learns nothing specific.
whyNot.2: Helped out and various things are vague.

B.q: A lab lost Gabriela's blood sample, and she had to pay for a repeat draw. Which sentence for her email to the lab has the most appropriate tone?
options: Your careless lab lost my sample. Great job, everyone.
Please waive the fee for my repeat blood draw on May 3.
Sorry to bother you, but maybe, if it's okay, could you check?
Refund me today or I will post about your awful lab online.
B.why: It is firm and courteous: a clear, specific request with no insults.

whyNot.0: Insulting (careless) and sarcastic (great job), and it makes no request.
whyNot.2: Timid and vague: it never says what should be checked or done.
whyNot.3: Demanding and threatening, which is unprofessional.

B.q: Which sentence for a nursing school essay avoids clichés?
options: At the end of the day, nurses are the backbone of patient care.
When push comes to shove, nurses step up to the plate.
Nurses coordinate care among doctors, patients, and families.
Nurses think outside the box to keep their patients safe.
B.why: It makes a specific point in fresh, direct words.

whyNot.0: “At the end of the day” and “the backbone of” are clichés.
whyNot.1: “When push comes to shove” and “step up to the plate” are clichés.
whyNot.3: “Think outside the box” is a cliché.

options: The firemen responded to the alarm within minutes.
The fire department's manpower responded within minutes.
The male and lady firefighters responded within minutes.
The firefighters responded to the alarm within minutes.
B.why: Firefighters is a gender-neutral job title.

whyNot.0: Firemen is a gendered job title; use firefighters.
whyNot.1: Manpower is gendered; use staff or crew.
whyNot.2: Mentioning gender is irrelevant here, and lady is not parallel with male.

C.q: A nurse is writing home-care instructions for the parent of a toddler. Which sentence is most appropriate?
options: Administer 5 mL PO q6h PRN for pyrexia.
Give 5 mL by mouth every 6 hours as needed for fever.
Just give the kiddo a bit of medicine whenever it seems needed.
Medication should be utilized at appropriate intervals as indicated.
C.why: Plain, specific words (amount, route, timing, reason) suit a parent who is not a clinician.

whyNot.0: Clinical abbreviations and jargon (PO, q6h, PRN, pyrexia) are unclear to a parent.
whyNot.2: Slang (kiddo) and vague wording (a bit, whenever) are unsafe and imprecise.
whyNot.3: Inflated (utilized) and vague (appropriate intervals): it never gives the dose or timing.

C.q: A recommendation letter describes an applicant who keeps working toward her goals despite setbacks. Which word best fits the letter's positive purpose?
options: persistent
stubborn
intractable
pigheaded
C.why: Persistent has a positive connotation: steady effort toward a goal.

whyNot.1: Stubborn suggests unreasonable refusal to change, a negative connotation.
whyNot.2: Intractable means hard to manage or control, a negative connotation.
whyNot.3: Pigheaded is a negative, insulting slang word.

C.q: Which revision of “We will utilize the facilitation of a dialogue to ascertain patient needs” is clearest for a clinic newsletter?
options: We will utilize dialogue to ascertain patient needs.
We will facilitate a dialogue to ascertain needs.
We will talk with patients to learn their needs.
We will chat it up with patients about their stuff.
C.why: Plain verbs (talk, learn) replace inflated ones and keep the full meaning.

whyNot.1: Still inflated (facilitate, ascertain), and it drops the word patient.
whyNot.3: Slang (chat it up) and vague wording (stuff) are too casual for a newsletter.

reteach.title: Tone is your voice on paper
reteach.question: On the phone, people judge you by your tone of voice before they judge your words. What does the reader “hear” in your writing when they cannot hear your voice?

blocks.h: The reader hears your word choice
blocks.body: On paper, your word choice is your tone of voice. “Your website is a joke” is shouting. “Sorry, maybe, if it's okay” is mumbling. “Please reschedule my exam” is a calm, clear voice. Slang sounds like talking to friends, jargon sounds like talking to coworkers, and inflated words sound like someone trying to impress. Choose the voice your reader needs to hear.

rows.label: Precise
values: We will use the new form.

blocks.text: More syllables do not mean a better answer. “Use” beats “utilize,” and “find out” beats “ascertain,” whenever the shorter word means the same thing.

explain.body: Professional tone is respectful and steady. In a complaint it is firm (facts and a clear request) and courteous (no insults, sarcasm or threats).

test.q: Which sentence keeps a firm but courteous tone in a complaint about a billing error?
options: Your billing department clearly can't do basic math.
Please correct the duplicate charge on my May statement.
I guess mistakes happen, so maybe look into it sometime?
I am outraged and disgusted by this unbelievable error!
test.why: It identifies the exact problem and asks for a fix, politely and without insults.

whyNot.0: Insulting and sarcastic; it also makes no request.
whyNot.2: Too timid and vague: it names no error and asks for no clear fix.
whyNot.3: Exaggerated, emotional language with no specific request.

explain.body: Slang is casual group language. Clichés are overused phrases (at the end of the day). Jargon is specialist vocabulary. All three weaken formal writing for a general reader.

options: The new schedule reduced overtime for night staff.
Our team finished the safety audit two days early.
Patients waited an average of ten minutes today.
The new nurse hit the ground running on day one.
test.why: “Hit the ground running” is an overused stock phrase.

whyNot.0: Plain, specific wording with no stock phrase.
whyNot.1: Plain, specific wording with no stock phrase.
whyNot.2: Plain, specific wording with a precise figure.

explain.body: Words with the same dictionary meaning can carry different feelings. Pick the one whose connotation matches your purpose, and prefer specific nouns and strong verbs to vague ones.

test.q: Which word has the most positive connotation?
options: thrifty
cheap
stingy
tightfisted
test.why: Thrifty praises careful use of money.

whyNot.1: Cheap suggests low quality or meanness with money.
whyNot.2: Stingy suggests an unwillingness to share or spend.
whyNot.3: Tightfisted is a negative, informal word for stingy.

explain.body: Name the person before the condition, describe equipment as something a person uses, and use gender-neutral titles.

options: a wheelchair-bound patient
a patient confined to a wheelchair
a patient who uses a wheelchair
a wheelchair patient
test.why: It names the patient first and presents the wheelchair as a tool the patient uses.

whyNot.0: Wheelchair-bound suggests the person is trapped.
whyNot.1: Confined suggests the person is imprisoned by the chair.
whyNot.3: It labels the person by the equipment.
